pages.content:
Pandas is a library in Python used for data manipulation and analysis. 

Interestingly Pandas is built on NumPy but focuses on labeled data and provides more high-level data manipulation tools. Pandas utilizes Series and DataFrame - new data structures that we will learn during this course.

If you are well-versed with Python - carry on!

If you need a refresher on Python or you have never used Python, we'd suggest you to go and check out our interactive and practical course on [Learn Python](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/python)

practiceProblems.title: Pandas vs NumPy
practiceProblems.description:
**Scenario 1**: You're analyzing the daily temperatures of a city for a month. You want to calculate the average temperature and convert all temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit.

NumPy is ideal for this task because:
- We're working with a simple numerical array.
- We need to perform element-wise mathematical operations.
- We don't need labeled data or complex data structures.

**Scenario 2**: You have sales data for different products over a week. You want to calculate the total sales for each product and find the best-selling product.

Pandas is better for this task because:
- We're working with structured data (products and their daily sales).
- We need to perform analysis on labeled data.
- We want to easily access and manipulate data by column names or indices.

You can check out the code implementation in the IDE for both the scenarios above. Over the course of the next few topics, we will learn how to implement Pandas.

If you want to go ahead and learn / revise NumPy - you can check out our learning path on NumPy [here](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/numpy)

practiceProblems.title: Creating Series
practiceProblems.description:
A Pandas Series is a one-dimensional array that can hold data of any type.

Series can be created from various data types including lists, numpy arrays, and dictionaries. Check the sample syntax below
```python
# From list
s1 = pd.Series([1, 3, 5, 7, 9])

s2 = pd.Series(np.array([1, 3, 5, 7, 9]))

# From dictionary
s3 = pd.Series({'a': 1, 'b': 3, 'c': 5})
```

- NumPy array - [0.5, 0.3, 0.8, 0.6]

practiceProblems.title: Understanding Pandas Series Indexing
practiceProblems.description:
Series have attributes like index, values, and dtype.

Index and Datatype - this is something that we have seen in lists as well as NumPy arrays
```python
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print(s[2])        # Output - 30
print(s.dtype)     # Output - int64
```

We can also use the custom labels for each element in the Series. 
```python
s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], index=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'])
print(s['c'])      # Output - 3
```
- Purpose: The index provides a label for each element in the Series, allowing you to access elements by these labels instead of just by their position.
- Structure: The index is a separate array-like object that runs parallel to the data in the Series. In this case, it's a list of strings: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'].
- Alignment and Access: Each label in the index corresponds to a value in the Series. So 'a' corresponds to 1, 'b' to 2, and so on.

Here's a visual representation of the Series:
```python
Index | Value
------|------
  a   |   1
  b   |   2
  c   |   3
  d   |   4
  e   |   5
```

### Task
We have given you a series of student grades. \
Output the scores for Bob and David to the console on separate lines using the index labels.

practiceProblems.title: Slicing series
practiceProblems.description:
Series can be indexed and sliced using labels or integer locations.
```python
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 50], index=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'])
print(s[1:4])
print(s['a':'d'])
```
gives us the following output
```python
b    20
c    30
d    40
dtype: int64
a    10
b    20
c    30
d    40
dtype: int64
```
- **Note:** When you use label-based slicing, the behavior includes both the start and the end labels, which is more intuitive when working with labeled data, such as dates or strings.

practiceProblems.title: Pandas DataFrame
practiceProblems.description:
A DataFrame is a 2-dimensional labeled data structure in Pandas. It can be thought of as a table or a spreadsheet-like structure where data is organized in rows and columns.

A common practical application for pandas DataFrames is in analyzing and manipulating structured data, such as sales records, financial data, or scientific observations.

We have populate the syntax for a dataframe creation in the IDE. Run the code to see the output.

### When to Use DataFrames vs Series
Use DataFrames when:
- You have multiple related columns of data (like in our sales example).

practiceProblems.title: Viewing data in DataFrames
practiceProblems.description:
Pandas provides several methods to inspect and view data in DataFrames. These methods are crucial for understanding your data, especially when working with large datasets.

head() and tail() - These methods show the first or last n rows of the DataFrame.

info() - This method provides a concise summary of the DataFrame, including column names, non-null counts, and data types.

Sample syntax below
```python
# Create a sample DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie', 'David', 'Eve', 'Frank', 'Grace', 'Henry'],
    'Age': [25, 30, 35, 28, 32, 40, 37, 33],
    'City': ['New York', 'San Francisco', 'Los Angeles', 'Chicago', 'Boston', 'Miami', 'Seattle', 'Denver']
})

# head() by default shows the first 5 rows. head(n) can be used to view n rows
print(df.head())

# View the last 3 rows
print(df.tail(3))

# Get information about the DataFrame
df.info()
```

- The last 5 rows

pages.title: Overview - Data cleaning and pre-processing
pages.content:
Imagine you're a data analyst for a large e-commerce company. You've been tasked with analyzing customer purchase behavior to improve marketing strategies. 

You receive a dataset containing customer information and purchase history, but it's far from perfect:
- Some customers' ages are missing or unrealistic (e.g., 200 years old).
- Purchase dates are in different formats (e.g., "2023-01-01", "01/01/2023", "Jan 1, 2023").
- Column names are inconsistent and unclear (e.g., "cust_id", "CustomerName", "purch_amt").
- There are duplicate entries for some transactions.
- Product categories are misspelled or inconsistent (e.g., "Electronics", "electronic", "Elctrnics").

Without proper cleaning and preprocessing, your analysis would be flawed:
- Missing age data could skew demographic insights.
- Inconsistent date formats would make time-based analysis impossible.
- Unclear column names would make the data hard to work with.
- Duplicate entries could lead to overestimated sales figures.
- Inconsistent categories would result in fragmented product analysis.

By cleaning and preprocessing this data, you ensure that your subsequent analysis is accurate, reliable, and truly representative of customer behavior, leading to more effective marketing strategies.

Let us dive into some basics of Data cleaning / Preprocessing using NumPy and Pandas in this module.

practiceProblems.title: Identifying Missing Data
practiceProblems.description:
In pandas, missing data can be represented in several ways:
- None: This is a Python singleton object used to represent the absence of a value.
- NaN (Not a Number): This is a special floating-point value defined by the IEEE 754 standard.
- NaT (Not a Time): This is used for missing datetime values.

Pandas treats None, NaN, and NaT as missing in most operations. We use isnull() or isna() to check for missing values:
```python
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, np.nan, 4],
                   'B': [5, np.nan, np.nan, 8],
                   'C': ['a', 'b', 'c', None]})

print(df.isnull())  # Boolean mask of missing values
print(df.isnull().sum())  # Count of missing values per column
```
Gives us the output
```python
       A      B      C
0  False  False  False
1  False   True  False
2   True   True  False
3  False  False   True
A    1
B    2
C    1
dtype: int64
```

### Task
Create a function that takes a DataFrame as input and returns the percentage of missing values in each column.

practiceProblems.title: Dropping missing data
practiceProblems.description:
Pandas provides several methods to drop missing data, primarily through the dropna() function. \
Remember, dropna() treats both None and NaN as missing values.

Here are the main approaches:
```python
# Drop rows with any missing values
df_clean = df.dropna()

# Drop rows only if all values are missing
df_clean = df.dropna(how='all')

# Drop rows with less than 2 non-null values
df_clean = df.dropna(thresh=2)

# Drop rows where column 'A' has missing values
df_clean = df.dropna(subset=['A'])

# Drop rows where either 'A' or 'B' is missing
df_clean = df.dropna(subset=['A', 'B'], how='any')
```
Note: 
- The dropna(thresh=n) method in pandas drops rows that have fewer than n non-null values
- `df_clean = df.dropna(subset=['A', 'B'])` will drop rows where either 'A' OR 'B' (or both) have missing values.
- `df_clean = df.dropna(subset=['A', 'B'], how='all')` drops rows only if ALL specified columns are null.
- Remember, dropna(subset=[...]) focuses on specific columns, ignoring the status of other columns not mentioned in the subset.

practiceProblems.description:
During data cleaning - while one option is to remove rows containing missing values - another is to fill missing data with values. Pandas provides several methods to fill missing data. Here are the main approaches:
```python
# Fill all missing values with 0
df_filled = df.fillna(0)

# Fill different values for different columns
df_filled = df.fillna({'A': 0, 'B': 99, 'C': 'Unknown'})

# Forward fill - This method propagates the last valid observation forward to next missing value
df_ffilled = df.ffill()

# Backward fill - This method uses the next valid observation to fill the gap.
df_bfilled = df.bfill()

# You can fill missing values with statistical measures like mean, median, or mode.
df['A'].fillna(df['A'].mean(), inplace=True)
df['B'].fillna(df['B'].median(), inplace=True)
```

- Data Type: Ensure the fill value is compatible with the column's data type.

pages.title: Datatype conversion - why is it required
pages.content:
Imagine you're a data analyst for an e-commerce company. You've been tasked with analyzing sales data to identify trends and make recommendations for inventory management and marketing strategies.

When you load the data into pandas, you notice some issues:
```python
order_id                object
date                    object
product_id              object
quantity                object
unit_price              object
total_sales             object
customer_age            object
is_returning_customer   object
dtype: object

  order_id        date product_id quantity unit_price total_sales customer_age is_returning_customer
0   OD1001  2023-01-15      P1234       2     $19.99     $39.98          35.0                  TRUE
1   OD1002  2023-01-15      P5678       1     $24.99     $24.99          28.0                 FALSE
2   OD1003  2023-01-16      P9876       3     $9.99      $29.97          42.0                  TRUE
3   OD1004  2023-01-16      P5432       1     $49.99     $49.99            -                  FALSE
4   OD1005  2023-01-17      P1234       2     $19.99     $39.98          31.0                  TRUE
```
- All columns are of type 'object' (string).
- Numeric columns (quantity, unit_price, total_sales, customer_age) are stored as strings.
- date is stored as a string, not a datetime object.
- is_returning_customer is stored as 'TRUE'/'FALSE' strings, not boolean.
- Some customer_age values are '-' instead of numbers.

The above issues will impact the following
- Incorrect Calculations - for example - you cannot sum strings to compute revenue
- Inefficient Storage - Storing numbers as strings uses more memory than storing them as integers or floats
- Date Operations - You can't perform date arithmetic or extract components (like month) easily
- Statistical Analysis - Functions like mean, median, etc., won't work on string data

In real-world data analysis, the ability to properly handle and convert data types is crucial.

The most straightforward method to convert from other datatypes to numeric is using astype().

pd.to_numeric() provides more control over error handling with options for errors:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({

})

```

practiceProblems.description:
Categorical data in pandas is used for
- Memory efficiency, especially for strings with repeated values
- Improved performance for certain operations
- Meaningful representation of non-numeric data with a specific set of possible values

The memory efficiency of categorical data in pandas stems from its internal representation. Categorical data in pandas is represented internally using two main components:
- Categories Array: A unique array of all possible category values.
- Codes Array: An integer array where each integer is an index pointing to a value in the categories array.

Let's consider a column with 1 million rows, containing only the values 'Apple', 'Banana', and 'Cherry'.
- Without Categorical: \
Each string is stored separately. \
Memory usage ≈ (5 + 6 + 6) bytes * 1,000,000 ≈ 17 MB \
(Assuming each character takes 1 byte and accounting for Python's string overhead)
- With Categorical: \
Categories Array: ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry'] ≈ 17 bytes \
Codes Array: 1,000,000 integers (1 byte each if using uint8) ≈ 1 MB \
Total: ≈ 1 MB

The primary function for converting to datetime is pd.to_datetime()

Pandas can automatically parse many date formats, but you can specify the format for ambiguous cases
```python
# American format (month/day/year)
```

```python
dates = ['2023-07-15', 'Invalid Date', '2023-07-17']
```

pages.title: Renaming and reordering columns - Overview
pages.content:
Imagine you're a data analyst at a retail company that recently acquired another company. \
Your task is to merge and analyze sales data from both companies' systems. \
However, each company used different column names in their sales reports.

```python
Company A:
         DATE PROD_ID PROD_NAME  QTY  UNIT_PRICE  TOT_REV
0  2023-01-01    A001    Widget  100       10.99   1099.0
1  2023-01-02    A002    Gadget  150       24.99   3748.5
2  2023-01-03    A001    Widget  120       10.99   1318.8

Company B:
     SaleDate ProductCode      ProductName  Quantity  Price  Revenue
0  2023-01-01        B001      Thingamajig        75  15.99  1199.25
1  2023-01-02        B002        Doohickey        50  19.99   999.50
2  2023-01-03        B003  Whatchamacallit        60   8.99   539.40
```
In this scenario, renaming columns is crucial for several reasons:
- Consistency: The two companies used different naming conventions (e.g., 'DATE' vs 'SaleDate'). Renaming ensures consistency across the merged dataset.
- Clarity: Some column names were ambiguous or used abbreviations (e.g., 'QTY', 'PROD_ID'). Renaming makes the data more immediately understandable.
- Merging Data: To concatenate or merge the DataFrames, having matching column names is essential. Without renaming, the merge would be difficult or impossible.

practiceProblems.title: Reordering columns
practiceProblems.description:
Reordering columns in Pandas is the process of changing the order in which columns appear in a DataFrame. This operation is purely structural and doesn't affect the data within the columns. 

One of the most straightforward methods is indexing with a list of column names.
You create a list of column names in the desired order and use it to index the DataFrame.
```python
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3], 'B': [4, 5, 6], 'C': [7, 8, 9]})
df_reordered = df[['C', 'A', 'B']]
```
gives us the output 
```python
   C  A  B
0  7  1  4
1  8  2  5
2  9  3  6
```
Reordering and Selecting Columns: You can combine reordering with column selection to keep only specific columns in a desired order.
```python
selected_columns = ['C', 'A']
df_selected = df[selected_columns]
```
gives us the output
```python
   C  A
0  7  1
1  8  2
2  9  3
```

### Task
You have a DataFrame df with columns 'ID', 'Name', 'Age', 'City', and 'Salary'. Perform the following operations:
- Reorder the columns to have 'Name' first, followed by 'Age', 'Salary' and 'City'.
- We have given a list containing the countries - add a new column 'Country' at the end.

### Expected output
```python
      Name  Age  Salary      City
0    Alice   25   50000  New York
1      Bob   30   60000    London
2  Charlie   35   70000     Paris
      Name  Age  Salary      City Country
0    Alice   25   50000  New York     USA
1      Bob   30   60000    London      UK
2  Charlie   35   70000     Paris  France
```

practiceProblems.description:
Duplicate rows in a DataFrame are rows that have the same values across all columns or a subset of columns. 

Methods for Identifying Duplicates

   - The original row is not flagged as a duplicate. Only the next instance of the exact same values are flagged as duplicate
- Using duplicate_subset parameter: You can specify a subset of columns to consider when identifying duplicates.
   - Note that only the specific column value is considered when identifying duplicates

- Note that based on Column 'A' - the values 2 and 3 are duplicate. Hence row index 2, 5 and 6 are flagged as duplicate

practiceProblems.title: Removing Duplicate Rows
practiceProblems.description:
Once duplicates are identified, you often want to remove them to clean your data. Pandas provides methods to easily remove duplicate rows while giving you control over which duplicates to keep.

Using drop_duplicates() method removes all duplicate rows and returns a new DataFrame. Note that the original data is retained - only duplicate rows are removed.
```python
df_unique = df.drop_duplicates()
```
You can specify which duplicate to keep using the keep parameter.
```python
# Keep first occurrence of duplicates
df_keep_first = df.drop_duplicates(keep='first')

# Keep last occurrence of duplicates
df_keep_last = df.drop_duplicates(keep='last')
```
You can use the subset parameter to specify columns for considering duplicates.
```python
# Remove duplicates based only on column 'A'
df_unique_A = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['A'])
```

### Task
We have populated a DataFrame with columns 'Student_ID', 'Name', and 'Grade'. \
The DataFrame has duplicate entries for some students with different grades. 
- Remove duplicates based on 'Student_ID', keeping the entry with the highest grade for each student. In order to get the highest grade for each student - you will have to first sort the dataframe with Student_ID and Grade in descending order.

### Expected output
```python
   Student_ID     Name  Grade
3           1    Alice     88
1           2      Bob     92
2           3  Charlie     78
5           4    David     95
```

pages.content:
Imagine you're a data analyst for an e-commerce company. The company has sales data from multiple products across various regions, and the management wants to understand sales performance to make informed decisions about inventory, marketing, and expansion.

- group.size(): Count the number of items in each group

- group.min(), group.max(): Find minimum and maximum values in each group
- group.agg(): Apply multiple aggregation functions at once

practiceProblems.title: Merging DataFrames
practiceProblems.description:
DataFrames can be merged based on the following types
- Inner Join: Returns only the rows that have matching values in both DataFrames.
- Left Join: Returns all rows from the left DataFrame and matching rows from the right DataFrame.
- Right Join: Returns all rows from the right DataFrame and matching rows from the left DataFrame.
- Outer Join: Returns all rows when there's a match in either left or right DataFrame.
```python
# Sample DataFrames
df1 = pd.DataFrame({'ID': [1, 2, 3], 'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'ID': [2, 3, 4], 'Score': [85, 90, 95]})

# Merge DataFrames
merged = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='ID', how='inner')
print(merged)
merged1 = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='ID', how='left')
print(merged1)
merged2 = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='ID', how='right')
print(merged2)
```

practiceProblems.title: Pivot tables
practiceProblems.description:
A pivot table is a data summarization tool that can automatically sort, count, total, or give the average of the data stored in one table or spreadsheet. In Pandas, the pivot_table() function allows you to create pivot tables from your DataFrames.

Key Concepts of Pivot Tables
- Index: The column(s) to use to make new frame's index. If None, uses existing index.
- Columns: Column(s) to use to make new frame's columns.
- Values: Column(s) to use for populating new frame's values.
- Aggregation Function: Function to use for aggregation, defaulting to numpy.mean.
```python
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Date': ['2023-01-01', '2023-01-01', '2023-01-02', '2023-01-02', '2023-01-03', '2023-01-03'],
    'Product': ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B', 'A', 'B'],
    'Sales': [100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350]
})

# Create a basic pivot table
pivot_table = pd.pivot_table(df, values='Sales', index='Date', columns='Product', aggfunc=np.sum)
```
```python
# Output
Product       A    B
Date                
2023-01-01  100  150
2023-01-02  200  250
2023-01-03  300  350
```
In the example above,
- We use 'Date' as the index (rows)
- 'Product' becomes our columns
- 'Sales' is the value we're aggregating
- We're using the sum function to aggregate sales

A Date Range in Pandas is a sequence of date-time indices. It's created using the pd.date_range() function, which generates a series of dates or timestamps at regular intervals. \

- end: The end date of the range
- periods: The number of periods to generate
- freq: The frequency of the date range (daily, monthly, etc.)

Frequency refers to the time interval between each date or time in a Date Range. Pandas supports various frequency aliases, allowing you to work with data at different time scales.

Common frequency aliases:
- D: Calendar day frequency
- B: Business day frequency
- W: Weekly frequency
- M: Month end frequency
- Q: Quarter end frequency
- Y: Year end frequency
- H: Hourly frequency
- T or min: Minute frequency
- S: Second frequency

practiceProblems.title: Resampling Time Series Data
practiceProblems.description:
Resampling is the process of changing the frequency of your time series data that allows you to:
- Aggregate data to a lower frequency (downsampling)
- Increase the frequency of your data (upsampling)
- Align multiple time series with different frequencies

Resampling is performed using the resample() method in Pandas, which is similar to groupby() but specifically designed for time series data.

Key Concepts
- Frequency: The target frequency for resampling (e.g., 'D' for daily, 'M' for monthly)
- Aggregation Function: The function used to combine values when downsampling (e.g., mean, sum, max)
- Fill Method: The method used to fill in missing values when upsampling (e.g., ffill, bfill)

We have updated some of the concepts in the IDE - go ahead and check the code to understand the function.

Here is how the following code works step by step for downsampling from daily to weekly with sum
```python
weekly_sum = daily_data.resample('W').sum()
```
- The resample('W') Method - 'W' is the frequency alias for weekly resampling.
- The Resampling Process - Pandas groups the daily data into weekly bins, Each bin starts on Monday and ends on Sunday (inclusive)
- The sum() Aggregation: After grouping the data into weekly bins, sum() is applied to each bin.
This calculates the sum of all daily values within each week.
- Result: weekly_sum. The resulting Series has a weekly frequency.
Each data point represents the sum of the daily values for that week.
The index of each point is the end of the week (Sunday).
